questions.q: How many members does EventName have?
questions.explain: Union holes produce the cross product: one member for every combination, 4 × 3 = 12. Adding a third hole multiplies again, which is how unions explode.

questions.q: What is the difference between `ORD-${number}` and `ORD-${1 | 2 | 3}`?
questions.explain: A hole with a primitive type such as string or number makes a pattern. A hole with literal types makes a finite union of literals.
options: None; both are unions of three strings
The first is a pattern that matches infinitely many strings; the second is a union of exactly three literals
The second is not allowed because template holes cannot contain unions

questions.q: Which string is not assignable to `${number}`?
questions.explain: `${number}` accepts strings that Number() can read as a number. Exponents, signs and hex all qualify. Numeric separators are only valid in source code: Number("1_500") is NaN.

questions.q: A checkout form types its amount field as `${number}`. Why is that not enough?
questions.explain: Types check the code you write, not the data users type. A money field needs a runtime check of its exact format, such as /^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/.
options: Because the type only exists in the browser
Because values from the form are runtime strings the compiler never sees, and even the type itself accepts " 42" and "1e3", which a money field should reject
Because template literal types cannot be used for object properties

questions.q: What is `flag:${boolean}`?
questions.explain: boolean is the union true | false, and null and undefined are also spelled out, so the hole expands to their literal spellings.

questions.q: What is `on${Capitalize<"paid" | "shipped">}`?
questions.explain: Capitalize uppercases the first character, and like the other intrinsic string types it applies to each member of a union.

questions.q: Why does function upper<S extends string>(text: S): Uppercase<S> need as Uppercase<S> in its body?
questions.explain: Intrinsic types have no runtime part, and the standard library types toUpperCase() as string. The assertion is where you take responsibility for the runtime matching the type, so test it.
options: Because toUpperCase does not exist on type parameters
Because text.toUpperCase() is typed as returning string; the function must promise that the runtime result matches the type
Because Uppercase is a runtime function that must be imported
It does not; TypeScript infers Uppercase<S> automatically

questions.q: Which value is assignable to Uppercase<string>?
questions.explain: On a non-literal string, Uppercase stays a pattern meaning "a string with no lowercase letters". Digits and dashes are unchanged by upper-casing, so "LAGOS-2" fits.

questions.q: status has type "paid" | "shipped". What is the type of name?
questions.explain: A template string expression is widened to string unless it is written with as const or in a place that expects a template literal type. `order.${status}` as const gives the precise union.

questions.q: Which line keeps name checked against the event name pattern?
questions.explain: An annotation with a template literal type gives the expression an expected type, so it is checked against the pattern. Concatenation with + and String() always produce string.

questions.q: Why does type Pin = `${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}` (with Digit = the ten digit strings) fail with TS2590?
questions.explain: The cross product of five ten-member unions is 105 members. Use a pattern, such as `${number}` plus a runtime length check, for shapes like PINs.
options: Because template literal types allow at most four holes
Because it would be a union of 100,000 strings, which is over the compiler's limit for union size
Because digits must be written as numbers
Because the same type is used twice in one template

questions.q: What is SplitName<"order.item.added">?
questions.explain: An infer followed by fixed text captures as little as possible, up to the first place the text matches. The last infer takes whatever is left.
questions.code: type SplitName<S> = S extends `${infer Entity}.${infer Action}` ? [Entity, Action] : [S];

questions.q: What is ParseAmount<"150000 kobo">?
questions.explain: infer Kobo extends number converts the captured text to a number literal type when the text is a valid number. For text such as "lots" the match fails and the result is never.
questions.code: type ParseAmount<S> = S extends `${infer Kobo extends number} kobo` ? Kobo : never;

questions.q: In S extends `${infer C}${infer Rest}`, what does C capture when S is "port"?
questions.explain: When an infer is followed directly by another infer, the first captures exactly one character. That is how types walk a string character by character, as in EnvName.

questions.q: With ParamNames from the lesson, what is ParamNames<"/shops/:shopId/orders/:orderId">?
questions.explain: Each step finds a :, captures the name up to the next / and recurses on the rest; the results are unioned. The mapped type Params then turns the names into { readonly shopId: string; readonly orderId: string }.

questions.q: The route type guarantees that params.orderId exists. What does it not guarantee?
questions.explain: The type is derived from the path, so it checks parameter names. The values come from the URL at runtime; the handler must still validate them and look them up.
options: That params.orderId names an order that exists, or has the right format
That the handler receives an object

questions.q: In the lesson's handler object type, why does the value use the original key N rather than the new name?
questions.explain: The as clause changes the key that appears in the new type, while N still refers to the key being visited. OrderEvents["onOrderPaid"] would not exist.
options: Because the new name is not available inside a mapped type
Because the payload is looked up in OrderEvents, whose keys are the event names; as only renames the resulting property
It is a mistake; it should be OrderEvents[HandlerName<N>]

questions.q: Why does the lesson allow wildcards in Grant but not in the needed argument of can(grants, needed)?
questions.explain: Grants describe what a role may do, so wildcards are useful there. A check guards one specific operation, such as refunds:approve; accepting orders:* there would let code ask a vaguer question than it means.
options: Because wildcards cannot be typed with template literal types
Because asking whether someone may do "anything to orders" is almost always a bug; a check should name one exact permission
Because * is not a valid string literal type
Because grants are stored in a database

questions.q: Grants are loaded from a database table. What protects the application from a grant row containing "order:read" (missing s)?
questions.explain: Types protect code you write. Data from storage is untyped until checked. as Grant[] would silence the compiler and let the bad grant through, where it silently grants nothing.
options: The Grant type, because the rows are assigned to Grant[]
A runtime check of every loaded grant, because database rows are plain strings the compiler never sees
Nothing is needed; the compiler checks the database

questions.q: What is Namespace<"order.paid" | "order.placed" | "stock.low">?
questions.explain: The conditional type distributes over the union, and a union holds each member once, so the two "order" results merge.
questions.code: type Namespace<N extends string> = N extends `${infer NS}.${string}` ? NS : never;
options: never, because the whole union does not match

questions.q: In bus.on("order.*", (event) => …), why must the handler check event.name before reading event.payload.totalKobo?
questions.explain: ShopEvent<Matching<"order.*">> is a discriminated union of { name, payload } objects. Reading a property that only one member has requires narrowing first. Properties all members share, like orderId, can be read directly.
options: Because event is a union of the three order events; only order.placed has totalKobo, and checking the name discriminant narrows the payload
Because payloads are only available after await

questions.q: The bus stores every handler as (event: ShopEvent) => void, with a cast. What makes that cast safe?
questions.explain: A function that only accepts order.paid events is not a function that accepts every event, which is why the compiler needs the cast. The invariant that makes it true lives in matches, so that function gets its own tests.
options: Nothing; the cast is only there to silence a warning
A handler for order.paid can handle every event, because TypeScript checks parameters loosely
The bus only calls a handler with events its pattern matches, so a handler for order.paid never receives another event; a test checks the matcher
Casts are always safe inside a module

questions.q: What does Exclude<`order.${OrderStatus}`, EventName> compute?
questions.explain: The template builds one name per status; Exclude keeps the ones that are not real event names. Demanding that this is never in a type test forces every status to have an event.
options: The event names that are not order events
The status-based order event names that have no entry in the event map
The order statuses that have no event
Every event name except the order ones

questions.q: Why does the inbox code use both satisfies readonly EventName[] on EVENT_NAMES and Expect<Equal<(typeof EVENT_NAMES)[number], EventName>>?
questions.explain: Each check catches one direction of drift. Without the Equal test, a new event added to ShopEvents but not to the list would be sent to the dead-letter queue.
options: They do the same thing; one is enough
satisfies rejects a name that is not an event; the Equal test rejects a list that misses one. Together, the runtime list and the type must match exactly
The Equal test validates messages at runtime

questions.q: A parameter is typed name: "order.placed" | "order.paid" | string so that unknown names are also accepted. What does the compiler see?
questions.explain: Every literal string is already a string, so the union simplifies to string. If you really must accept unknown names, write the escape hatch deliberately (for example EventName | (string & {})) and understand that it switches off typo checking.
options: A union of three members with autocomplete for the first two
Just string: the literals are absorbed, so typos are no longer caught

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The misspelt "order.payed" subscription never runs, and emitting an event nobody listens to just returns 0. With string names, both mistakes are silent.
options:
receipt sent
Error: unknown event order.refunded

questions.q: These strings are all written in `${number}`-style fields. What does this print?
questions.explain: Number() trims spaces, reads hex and exponents, rejects numeric separators and turns the empty string into 0. `${number}` follows almost the same rules (it rejects the empty string), which is why it is a poor validator.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: charAt(0) of an empty string is "", so nothing breaks. Only the first letter changes case, matching what the Capitalize type describes.

questions.q: At runtime, this code splits a name the way `${infer Entity}.${infer Action}` does. What does it print?
questions.explain: indexOf finds the first dot, just as the first infer captures up to the first match. The rest, dots included, goes to the action.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: pattern.slice(0, -1) removes only the *, keeping the dot, so the prefix is "order.". "orders.archived" and "order" do not start with it. Slicing off two characters would have matched "orders.archived" too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The supervisor's orders:* covers every order action, but for refunds they only have read. The cashier has no approve permission at all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The : is sliced off the parameter names, and each value is URL-decoded. The second URL has fewer segments than the pattern, so it does not match at all.

questions.q: This runtime function turns camelCase config keys into environment variable names. What does it print for the three keys?
questions.explain: Every capital letter gets its own underscore, so an acronym is split letter by letter. The type-level EnvName from the lesson makes the same choice; if you want SMS_API_KEY, both the type and the function must change, and a test should pin them together.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: includes on the list of names accepts only exact members. Unlike an in check on an object, it does not accept inherited names such as "toString".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Handlers run in subscription order. order.shipped matches the entity wildcard, the exact name and the global wildcard. A payment event only reaches *.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: as const only changes the compile-time type (to "order.paid" | "order.shipped"). At runtime both are ordinary strings with the same characters, so they are equal and typeof says "string".

questions.q: Finish capitalize so it uppercases only the first character and returns the matching Capitalize<S> type. The program should print onOrderPaid onStockLow.
questions.explain: charAt(0) is safe on an empty string, where text[0] would be undefined. The single as promises that the runtime result matches the intrinsic type.

questions.q: Finish matches(pattern, name): "*" matches everything, "order.*" matches every name that starts with order., and anything else must be equal. The program should print true true false false.
questions.explain: Keep the dot in the prefix (slice(0, -1) removes only the *), otherwise order.* would also match a future orders.archived.

questions.q: Finish can(grants, needed). A grant matches when it is "*", the exact permission, or resource:* for the permission's resource. The program should print true false true.
questions.explain: The types stop typos and wildcard checks at compile time; the function decides at runtime. Take the resource from the permission being checked, never from the grant.

questions.q: Finish matchRoute(path, url). Split both on /; if the lengths differ return null; a segment starting with : captures the decoded URL segment under its name; any other segment must be equal. The program should print { shopId: 'ada', orderId: 'ORD-9' } null.
questions.explain: This is the runtime half of the typed router. The ParamNames type computes the same names from the path at compile time, so the handler gets a precise params type.

questions.q: Finish handlerName, the runtime version of `on${Capitalize<Entity>}${Capitalize<Action>}`. Split the event name at the first dot and capitalize both parts. The program should print onOrderPaid onPaymentFailed.
questions.explain: The type and the function describe the same naming rule twice. Split at the first dot, as the first infer does, and test both against a table of expected names.

questions.q: Finish isEventName as a type guard backed by the EVENT_NAMES list, then use it to sort the incoming names. The program should print accepted: order.paid,stock.low dead-letter: order.refunded,toString.
questions.explain: Widening the readonly tuple to readonly string[] lets includes accept any string without a cast on the argument. Names from outside are checked against the same list the type is derived from.

questions.q: Finish envName so each capital letter gets an underscore in front and the whole name is upper-cased. The program should print PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY DATABASE_URL PORT.
questions.explain: A replace callback inserts the underscore before each capital, then toUpperCase finishes the job. The lesson's EnvName<S> type does the same one character at a time, so config code can type process.env[envName(key)] lookups precisely.
